item.title: Friendship paradox: Why young people feel ‘too connected to connect’
item.description: Many report struggling to build friendships that provide a genuine sense of closeness, belonging and support.
item.content:encoded:
You know what’s happening in the lives of dozens of people. A friend from school has just had a baby. Someone you follow online recently got engaged. A colleague has returned from a holiday. Messages and updates arrive constantly. Yet when you’re having a difficult week, deciding who to call feels surprisingly hard. You’re connected – but you don’t feel it.

This paradox is increasingly familiar to many young adults. Despite being more connected than any previous generation, many report struggling to build friendships that provide a genuine sense of closeness, belonging and support. Young people have been described as “too connected to connect”.

You might feel you have more connections than ever before, but those connections can feel shallow, rushed and carefully staged. Relationships abound, but authenticity – the ability to be yourself – feels scarce.

In my own work, I’ve seen this in children who contort themselves into particular roles or identities to preserve family connection. Or in spouses and partners who hide parts of themselves to maintain a facade or status quo in a marriage or romantic relationship.

In essence, it is a form of conditional love: the idea that we are only lovable if we present particular sides of ourselves, while keeping others carefully edited or hidden away....

item.title: ‘Regime Change’: This book about Donald Trump’s second term is essential, chilling reading
item.description: Trump has also, according to the book and exhaustive reporting by journalists, abused his power to enrich himself and his family.
item.content:encoded:
Not long after the Second World War, the Jewish, German-born political philosopher Leo Strauss coined the term reductio ad Hitlerum. It suggests that simply comparing something to Adolf Hitler does not inevitably taint it with the Nazi dictator’s terrible crimes. Hitler was a vegetarian, but that doesn’t make all vegetarians bad people.

When the internet arrived several decades later, attorney Mike Godwin updated Strauss. “As an online discussion grows longer,” he said, “the probability of a comparison involving Nazis or Hitler” increases.

These days, few are willing to compare anyone or anything to Hitler, for fear of invalidating their argument. This can have the effect of closing off comparisons that could be illuminating.

Nowhere is this more strikingly illustrated than in the closing scene of Regime Change – Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s excellent, glowingly reviewed book about the first year of the second Trump administration – in which the authors finally gain an interview with the president to fact-check the damning material they have gathered.

Haberman has been reporting on Trump since his New York property developer days, and Swan has covered both his presidencies. The New York Times journalists knew from experience that Trump had two main modes of dealing with journalists: silk-smooth salesman’s patter and outright bullying.

item.title: Bangladesh to Nepal, revolutions toppled regimes but lasting change is elusive
item.description: Gen Z movements are swift and successful but struggle to do the slow work of institutional transformation.
item.content:encoded:
Two years after Bangladesh’s July uprising, the country’s greatest political lesson is no longer about how an authoritarian government fell.

It is about why replacing a government proved far easier than rebuilding a state. This is not simply Bangladesh’s story. It is becoming the defining political paradox of Generation Z across the world.

From Dhaka to Kathmandu, from Tunis to Colombo, young people have demonstrated an extraordinary ability to mobilise millions, but a much more limited ability to translate revolutionary momentum into durable institutional change.

The question is no longer whether young people can bring down governments. They clearly can. The real question is whether they can redesign the machinery of the state after the celebration ends.

The July uprising will remain one of the most remarkable moments in Bangladesh’s democratic history. Millions of citizens, led largely by students and young activists, united behind a simple objective.

The movement gathered enormous public sympathy after the killing of Abu Sayeed, whose death became a powerful symbol of state violence. Within weeks, a government that had ruled for fifteen years collapsed under unprecedented public pressure.

item.title: Israel says it will probe 2024 killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza

The Israeli military on Wednesday said that it is launching a criminal investigation into the 2024 killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab in Gaza, AP reported.

In January 2024, Rajab and her family were fleeing Gaza city when their vehicle was allegedly shelled by the Israeli forces. Rajab was trapped inside the car and found dead 12 days later after Israeli forces withdrew from the area. Six of her family members and two paramedics who were trying to rescue them were also killed.

Research agency Forensics Architecture and audio investigations group Earshot said that they mapped 335 bullet holes on the body of the car.

Rajab’s killing became a global symbol of the suffering faced by the children in Gaza because of the conflict.

item.title: Indian stock market least-preferred in Asia, shows survey
item.description: One-third of fund managers were allocating a smaller share of their portfolios to Indian equities, the findings showed.
item.content:encoded:
India is now Asia’s least-preferred stock market, replacing Indonesia, Bloomberg quoted a Bank of America survey of fund managers as having shown on Wednesday.

The Indian stock market has been one of the world’s worst performers this year.

The survey found that 32% of fund managers were allocating a smaller share of their portfolios to Indian stocks. The biggest concern among investors was that there are not enough listed Indian companies with a strong presence in the artificial intelligence sector, Bloomberg quoted the survey findings as saying.

Weak economic growth was the second-biggest concern. The lack of policy reforms to improve the business environment in the country and high valuations of the stocks have also contributed to the cautious view of Indian equities, the findings said.

The survey conducted between August 7 and August 13 received responses from 98 panellists managing $272 billion in assets.

Indian stocks have declined in the past two weeks despite an improving earnings forecast of companies, Bloomberg reported.

India was last ranked as the least-preferred market in Bank of America’s survey in May. At the time, rising energy costs had put pressure on the country’s growth outlook following the United States-Iran war, which spiked global crude oil prices.

item.title: Fiction: A family’s personal history from the Anglo-Sikh wars to the uneasy years of British rule
item.description: An excerpt from ‘For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died’, by Priya Hajela.
item.content:encoded:
When I talk about Henry Lawrence and Jeremiah Brasyer, the first thought that comes to most people’s minds is, “Those firangis, how can you have anything good to say about them, especially now when we’ve finally thrown them out?” But listen to the story and then decide for yourself what you think of these two British men.

It was July 2, 1857, two months into the Bengal Army uprising, two months of upended lives in a sweltering colony where natives and colonisers alike found their certainties crumbling. For the first time in over one hundred years, the British officers and civil servants who had assumed colonial rule to be their right and duty were afraid of what was going to happen to them.

They were ridiculously outnumbered as civilians, of course, but the Bengal Army was also over seventy per cent non-European. Over the years, as the British sought cushier roles, Indians stepped up to fill the ranks, drawn by secure pay and dashing uniforms, eventually gaining enough leverage to dictate terms around religious preferences. It verbally stated that if the Odisha Sentence Review Board did not decide on the matter by the next hearing, the court would take the decision.

Staines and his minor sons were burnt to death by a mob led by Singh in Odisha in January 1999 when they were sleeping in a jeep. The attackers had accused the missionary of illegal religious conversion.

High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi made the remarks at an event in Dhaka two days after a Bangladesh foreign ministry official said that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would not visit India until New Delhi extradited Sheikh Hasina.

The demonstration later snowballed into a broader agitation against her government.

item.description: The children had complained of a burning sensation in the throat and stomach pain after eating the meal at school in the Nalanda district.
item.content:encoded:
Thirty-four students of a government school in Bihar’s Nalanda district fell sick on Tuesday after eating a midday meal in which detergent powder was said to have been mistakenly added instead of salt, The Indian Express reported.

The students at the Middle School, Parasi, in the district’s Noorsarai block had complained of a burning sensation in their throats and stomach pain after eating the midday meal, The Hindu reported.

Nalanda Civil Surgeon Jai Prakash Singh said that they had suffered from food poisoning. Their health condition was stable, he added.

The headmaster of the school, Shailendra Kumar Singh, told reporters that the meal was supplied by a local non-governmental organisation, reported The Indian Express. It comprised rice and soyabean-potato curry as per the prescribed menu.

The school serves the midday meal in multiple sittings, Singh said. “During the second sitting, a student, identified as the granddaughter of a school cook, reportedly asked for additional salt,” the headmaster was quoted as saying by the newspaper. “The cook allegedly picked up detergent powder instead of salt by mistake and added it to the girl’s food.”

item.title: This book explores new methods of time management to boost personal productivity
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Inspired Leader: Seven Practices to Unlock Your Leadership Potential’, by Anil Sachdev.
item.content:encoded:
The most critical resource that we have is time. We all have limited time on this planet. How we make use of it determines the legacy that we create. Many of us know what truly matters to us, and yet we invest time in inconsequential activities. The distraction caused by our devices and social media is a significant cause that interferes with our desire to realise our full potential.

For example, we know that we need to put in a lot of time and effort to learn an important new skill, and yet we do not find the time to do so. Instead of taking responsibility for this, we keep blaming external factors for our failures. Many of us also suffer from procrastination. We keep putting off important work and fill our day with various distractions, which will not help us move towards our goals. Excessive Internet surfing, engaging in pointless debates, gossip and politicking are examples of time wasters.

item.title: Tamil Nadu increases maternity leave to one year for government employees having third child
item.description: In March, the state restricted maternity leave for those with two or more surviving children to 12 weeks.
item.content:encoded:
The Tamil Nadu government on Tuesday said it will increase the maternity leave for its employees having their third child to 365 days from 12 weeks, the Deccan Herald reported.

The state initially had 90 days of maternity leave for women government employees. This duration was later increased to six months in 2011, nine months in 2016, and one year in 2021 by successive governments led by the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam and the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam.

In March, the state government restricted maternity leave to 12 weeks for government employees with two or more surviving children by amending a provision in the state’s Fundamental Rules, which regulate working conditions, The New Indian Express. The decision was taken following a Supreme Court order.

In June, the Madras High Court upheld the provision while hearing the case of a government employee who had asked for 365 days of leave after she had her third child.

item.title: ‘Dimagi naxals’: The freedom to disagree is a political right – and is economically valuable
item.description: A country confident in its institutions does not need to fear every dissenting idea. It can allow the argument to take place and trust its citizens to judge.
item.content:encoded:
On Independence Day, Prime Minister Narendra Modi warned that while armed naxalism had largely been defeated, a different danger remained. He cautioned agains “dimagi naxals” – those who, he suggested, carry naxalite thinking in their minds. He said that they needed to be identified and isolated.

The political debate that followed has understandably focused on what exactly Modi meant and whom the phrase was intended to describe. But there is a more fundamental question worth asking: what happens when the state begins to distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate ideas?

This is not simply a question about freedom of speech. It is also a question about competition, information and the possibility of institutional error.

Richard Posner, in Economic Analysis of Law, offers an unexpectedly useful way of thinking about this. In his discussion of the protection of free markets in ideas and religion, he approaches freedom of expression through an economic intuition: ideas, like goods, benefit from competition. The state should therefore be cautious about intervening in the marketplace in which ideas compete. The analogy deserves to be taken seriously.

item.title: China passes law allowing it to target critics beyond its borders
item.description: The law on ethnic unity could be used to silence Chinese, Uyghur and Tibetan diaspora communities.
item.content:encoded:
On July 1, China brought into force its Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, converting a decade of Xi Jinping’s doctrine of “forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation” into binding law.

Most attention has gone to its domestic machinery: entrenching Mandarin over minority languages, unified state textbooks and “inter-embedded” neighbourhoods engineered to dilute concentrations of Uyghurs and Tibetans among the Han majority. In other words, this is an assimilationist project that’s already far advanced.

The provision that matters most to the world outside China is buried near the end. Article 63 declares that organisations and individuals outside Chinese territory who “undermine ethnic unity” or “create ethnic division” shall be pursued for legal liability.

The Chinese government is therefore asserting, in statute, that its authority follows its critics across oceans into other countries, including Canada, home to some of the world’s largest Chinese, Uyghur and Tibetan diaspora communities. The danger is not that the law reaches across borders. It is what it criminalises, whom it targets and how it’s enforced.

Getting the definition right

item.title: Some speed‑reading apps make big claims. But how fast can we actually read?
item.description: However, research has shown these apps have negligible effects on reading rates and can actually reduce comprehension.
item.content:encoded:
Some speed-reading advocates claim that with proper training (outlined in many popular books and YouTube videos) or the use of special apps, it’s possible to increase your reading rate to 1,000 words per minute or more.

Such books, videos and apps generally assume our reading speed is constrained because we are inefficient at extracting information from the printed page. But is this the case?

To assess these claims, let’s first see what the science says about our reading capacities.

A 2019 meta-analysis of 190 published studies found that when silently reading English non-fiction, adults read at a rate of 175–300 words per minute. Interestingly, this rate increased to 200–320 words per minute for fiction. This difference may reflect the fact that fiction tends to be more engaging or may be easier to understand.

Advocates of speed-reading, however, claim these estimates are conservative and reflect “bad reading habits”. But this contradicts what actually happens when we read.

How we read

During reading, our eyes don’t move smoothly across a printed page but instead make rapid movements called saccades, separated by brief pauses called fixations.

Although language processing continues during saccades, visual processing is suppressed. Information on the printed page is only extracted during fixations.

But as we approach the banks, the pungent smell of sewage hangs in the air, the water is thick with sludge, and just beyond the shoreline rises Kashmir’s largest dumping site – painting a completely different picture from the once-romanticised lake.

item.title: ‘Holy cow, filth and squalor’: Why India was unhappy with its image in Sweden in the 1960s
item.description: India’s diplomats blamed British media for Sweden’s unflattering coverage, even as a press attaché argued that Swedish journalism had its own logic.
item.content:encoded:
In the early decades after independence, India enjoyed warm diplomatic relations with Sweden and Denmark, both of which were keen to support newly decolonised countries with economic assistance. These friendly ties, however, did not translate into favourable coverage of India in the Scandinavian press.

In the 1960s, Indian diplomats in Copenhagen and Stockholm were increasingly frustrated by what they saw as a lack of balanced reporting on India. They believed much of the Scandinavian media relied too heavily on British and American news agencies, which, in their view, shaped an unflattering picture of the country.

“At present the Danish press is completely dependent on foreign news agencies, mainly British and American,” the Indian Embassy in Copenhagen wrote to the Ministry of External Affairs in 1964. The embassy noted that there were plans to establish a Scandinavian news agency and suggested reaching out to it in an effort to “combat anti-India propaganda” in the local press.

The concern was particularly acute in Sweden. item.title: This book shows that from the Cholas to the British, governing India was inseparable from religion
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The People’s Sanctum: The 100-Year Struggle to Democratise Temples in India’, by Manuraj Shunmugasundaram.
item.content:encoded:
The relationship between temples and the sovereign evolved over hundreds of years and has been one of great interest to scholars. Academics Arjun Appadurai and Carol A Breckenridge studied temples in Chennai and Madurai to show how the deity in a temple was considered to be the “paradigmatic sovereign”. The daily rituals followed in South Indian temples of Shiva and Vishnu are generally described as rājōpachāra, which refers to the paying of royal honours. With royal paraphernalia including palanquins, troupes of dancers and musicians and decoration of flowers, crowns and other jewellery, the deity was given the treatment typically reserved for royalty.

During processions and temple car (ther) festivals, the chief deity is still taken out into the streets around the temple, where worshippers gather to catch a glimpse, seek blessing and provide offerings. It is not unlike how royalty would engage with subjects. Beyond the realm of the temple, the deity is used to commanding resources “which are necessary and appropriate for the support and materialisation of the ritual process”. These resources, which include lands, jewellery and other forms of patronage, were usually received in the form of donations to the temple.

item.title: For weeks, an Assam district stared at drought. Then it got hit by floods
item.description: The paddy farmers of Golaghat could not sow the crop in June because of deficient rain. In July, their fields got inundated.
item.content:encoded:
June had come and gone. It was almost the end of July. But Babul Bora of eastern Assam’s Golaghat district was still waiting for rains to sow paddy.

This was unusual. Monsoon typically arrives in Assam in the first week of June. Between mid-June and mid-July, farmers across the region get busy in sowing and transplanting paddy.

“Khorang asile,” Bora told Scroll. “There was a drought.” The 56-year old cultivator from Balidowa village in Pachim Brahmaputra panchayat saw cracks appear in his fields.

Many other villages in Golaghat recorded such conditions. According to reports by district authorities, three of Golaghat’s six revenue circles faced “drought-like” conditions as of July 14.

Four days later, disaster struck.

On July 19, heavy rain caused the Gelabil river near Bora’s village to swell up, submerging homes and farmlands.

In the week between July 16 and 22, Golaghat received 147% more rain than usual, data from the India Meteorological Department shows.

Golaghat became one of the four worst-hit flood districts in Assam. Over 100 people have lost their lives and around seven lakh people displaced across the state in devastating floods. The waters have wreaked havoc in Upper Assam, areas which have rarely seen such intense floods in the past.

item.title: Food delivery workers to get minimum hourly wages for ‘engaged time’, say Australia’s new rules
item.description: It is the result of almost two years of negotiations between the Transport Workers’ Union and two major platforms, Uber Eats and DoorDash.
item.content:encoded:
From August 17, thousands of food delivery workers across Australia will benefit from new workplace protections – including new minimum hourly rates of pay.

That’s because on Tuesday, a new minimum standards order was handed down by an expert panel of the Fair Work Commission. The order covers “employee-like” workers at digital on-demand delivery platforms.

This is the first order of its kind, and as such it sets a benchmark for separate applications currently underway covering rideshare and parcel delivery workers.

It is the result of almost two years of negotiations between the Transport Workers’ Union and two major platforms, Uber Eats and DoorDash, through proceedings at the Fair Work Commission. While these groups ultimately managed to reach a consensus about the new protections, the reforms weren’t always warmly welcomed.

So, what’s actually changing for on-demand delivery workers? And what could it mean for the price of food deliveries?

The major change for food delivery workers is that the “interim” minimum standard order will create a new “earnings floor”. This won’t work in quite the same way as a minimum wage for employees.

Workers will be entitled to a minimum hourly rate for their “engaged time”: the period between accepting a delivery and completing it.

item.title: Restore E10 fuel option for older vehicles, says chief economic adviser
item.description: V Anantha Nageswaran said that India has up to 80 million older carburettor-based two-wheelers, which may run hotter due to petrol blended with 20% ethanol.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government should restore the option of 10% ethanol-blended fuel, or E10 fuel, at petrol pumps for older vehicles, Chief Economic Adviser V Anantha Nageswaran said in an article published in The Indian Express on Monday.

The government’s Ethanol Blended Petrol programme mandates that all petrol sold in the country be blended with 20% ethanol – a substance produced from sugarcane and food grain. The policy is aimed at reducing India’s dependency on fossil fuels, cutting greenhouse gas emissions and boosting income for sugarcane farmers.

However, consumers have complained that the new fuel mix damages engines and reduces their mileage.

Nageswaran and co-author Akash Poojari, a consultant with the Department of Economic Affairs, said that India has roughly 75 million to 80 million older two-wheelers that run on carburettors, which regulate the air-fuel mixture in an engine.

The carburettor-based engines cannot detect the additional oxygen in the E20 variant of petrol and adjust the fuel-air mixture accordingly, they said. As a result, the engine receives too little fuel for the amount of air drawn in, causing it to run hotter.

item.title: Should India be worried about the ‘AI bubble’?

The fortunes of millions of households in India, from those of software engineers to stock market investors, are increasingly tied to the same distant number: the valuation of seven American technology companies.

The S&P 500 – a stock market index tracking the largest publicly traded companies in the US – has climbed nearly 80% over five years, propelled largely by Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla.

An AI-driven surge has pushed their stocks to record highs. But the economic fundamentals underneath that surge should worry anyone who depends on the health of the global economy, including India.

‘AI bubble’

Data centres and AI-linked spending now account for a disproportionate share of American growth, helping the world’s largest economy remain resilient despite considerable headwinds.

Goldman Sachs predicts that spending on AI infrastructure, from data centres to chips, will rise from $765 billion this year to $1.6 trillion by 2031. Corporate adoption has surged too, with McKinsey finding that regular generative AI use has doubled since 2023, from about a third of firms to over two-thirds.

item.title: How the ‘Zed Beats’ music movement give Zambians back their voice
item.description: This blend of indigenous musical elements with international influences uses local languages, which has great resonance with young people.
item.content:encoded:
Zed Beats is a music movement that evolved in the late 1980s when young producers started using computers to blend western music with local languages and flavour. Today it’s an umbrella term for popular urban music in Zambia.

Musician and academic Mathew Tembo is a Zed Beats specialist. His PhD is on its history, production and musical labour from 1986 to 2024. We asked him to tell us about the music and how it shapes the country.

What is Zed Beats?

Zed Beats takes its name from the “Z” in “Zambia”. It’s a blend of indigenous musical elements with influences drawn from R&B, reggae, rap, Jamaican dancehall, hip-hop, Afrobeats, amapiano and other urban music genres trending at the time of its production.

The music, sung mostly in Zambian languages Chinyanja and Chibemba, along with some English, is produced on digital audio workstations by self-taught producers in home studios. The use of local languages makes Zed Beats resonate with young people, whose everyday conversations are carried out in these languages.

What forces created the ‘new’ music?

Indian writers have previously won the Booker Prize, which is restricted to works written in English: Salman Rushdie (1981), Arundhati Roy (1997), Kiran Desai (2006) and Aravind Adiga (2008). Chakravarty’s doctoral work was on the literature of the English Civil War of the 17th century. The complexity of South Asian gender and queer expressions can’t be contained by the Anglophone queer theorisation. First, because any such exercise makes one engage with South Asia’s rich and textured myth-historical past. Second, it’s this inheritance that renders the contemporary, contextual meaning to modern-day queerness, making the latter always in conversation with its past, enabling imagination of collective queer futures.

item.title: What the saga of Monsieur Mounissamy tells us about Franco-Indian identity
item.description: Pankaj Rishi Kumar’s documentary ‘To Die a Frenchman’ plunges into the hidden, intimate layers of colonial violence.
item.content:encoded:
If Gregor Samsa had been born in Pondicherry, he wouldn’t have awakened as a cockroach but as a chameleon. He would have been named accordingly, such as Jean-Grégoire Samoussapoullé, Grégoire Samikkannu, Grégorius Samassamy-Mudaliar, or, with a touch of aristocratic eccentricity, Grégoire-Marie Samassamy de Oulgaret.

Because of a colonial absurdity dating back to 1962, thousands of people find themselves in this Kafkaesque limbo, caught between two nations, two cultures, two identities, and two flags. They wake to the opening bars of La Marseillaise and go to sleep humming Jana Gana Mana. Their identity eludes both France and India, while the truly schizophrenic Franco-Pondicherrians sing neither anthem correctly. As the sun sets, they forsake both anthems for Marie, le pêcheur, an old Creole tune that drunkards sing off-key in the city’s countless bars. This timeless melody, appropriate for no nation, belongs to everyone and nowhere at once.

item.title: Upper Assam’s flood catastrophe is a direct result of river and mountain grabbing
item.description: Rampant mining and deforestation have shaken the very core of the region’s fragile ecologies.
item.content:encoded:
Since July 19, an artificial flood has wreaked havoc in four Upper Assam districts. So catastrophic has this flood been that nearly 800 villages and an area of around 1,19,000 hectares of cropland have been submerged, sheets of mud have been deposited in fields and inside people’s homes and large areas in the countryside have been turned into lakes.

More than 100 people have died and roughly seven lakh have been affected. Countless cattle have died.

The worst part of this disaster is that these are places not on the map of Assam’s annual flooding. But now, they seem to be doomed, as if a malignant wound has been created that will only spread and not heal.

For a land that is shaped and reshaped by the Brahmaputra river system and its unique fluvial dynamics, floods are not new in Assam – nor unwanted. Every monsoon, floodwaters bring alive all that was parched and dormant, replenishing the wetlands and the paddy fields, and reassuring fecundity in all living beings.

Assamese society has been traditionally a flood-dependent society, not a flood-fearing or flood-resisting one.

To make sense of the current catastrophe in Upper Assam, a historical understanding of how a natural phenomenon has become disastrous in the Brahmaputra Valley is necessary.

item.title: UK drought highlights precarious food system
item.description: Farmers are reporting dry soil and poor crop conditions while the country’s fresh produce depends on increasingly uncertain global supplies.
item.content:encoded:
Much of England is now officially in drought. Reservoir levels are being closely monitored by water companies, while farmers are reporting dry soils and poor crop conditions. Further restrictions such as grazing rules could soon come into effect.

Water is recognised as critical national infrastructure. However, drought does not only threaten our water supply. It also tests the resilience of the food system that depends on it.

For most of us, that reality becomes visible in the supermarket: standing in front of a shelf with no cucumbers, more expensive tomatoes or fewer fresh vegetables to choose from. These episodes have become increasingly familiar in recent years. We notice the empty shelves, accept the higher prices and move on.

But I keep wondering: why does this surprise so many people?

The UK carefully monitors many of the systems that underpin everyday life. We publish inflation figures every month, NHS waiting lists every week and regularly report on water reservoir levels because these indicators tell us whether essential systems are becoming stronger or weaker. They provide an early indication that intervention may be needed before problems escalate. Food, however, is different. We tend to judge the resilience of our food system only after something has gone wrong.

That seems odd for something so fundamental. Food is every bit as essential as healthcare, energy or water,...

item.title: ‘Sophie, Standing There’: After ‘Sorrow and Bliss’, Meg Mason’s new novel asks if books can save us
item.description: Author Meg Mason palpates the tender spots that linger in the wake of divorce, infertility, long-term job insecurity and even the wounds religion may inflict.

I sometimes say that My Family and Other Animals – Gerald Durrell’s autobiographical novel from 1956 – saved my life. My mother pressed her dog-eared copy into my hands during a year I was hospitalised repeatedly for major depression.

The sun-soaked Greek island of Corfu – as well as the Durrell family’s foibles and adventures – felt a world away from my hometown’s bleak winter and all those blister packets and doctors’ waiting rooms. I became fascinated by Durrell’s colourful childhood and his longstanding career as both an author and a naturalist. I could easily recall the story’s funniest moments and parrot the most memorable lines.

On even the hardest days, it somehow seemed to help.

This may seem like a roundabout way of introducing Sophie, Standing There, the new novel by New Zealand–born, Sydney-based Meg Mason, which centres on a soon-to-be-divorced festival worker and her fixation on an author whose work begins to speak to her. But this story, too, is about what books and authors can mean to us at particular times, and how they might save us – sometimes not only in their what but also in their when.

item.title: Rare Eurasian lynx recorded on camera traps in Sikkim

item.content:encoded:
A Eurasian lynx has been recorded in a camera-trap image from the Tso Lhamo plateau in Sikkim. This encounter marks the first confirmed photographic evidence of the species in the state. It is also the second such record from the Eastern Himalayas. The image, captured in January 2026 at an altitude of 5,250 metres in Mangan district, shows the animal moving across a rocky, sparsely vegetated high-altitude slope.

The sighting comes from a long-term snow leopard and rangeland monitoring programme led by the Sikkim forest department and WWF-India. The initiative tracks snow leopards and associated wildlife while studying the ecological condition of the trans-Himalayan rangelands.

The Sikkim record follows a 2025 photographic documentation of a Eurasian lynx in Arunachal Pradesh during a joint survey by WWF-India and the Arunachal Pradesh forest department.

“It highlights the ecological significance of our high-altitude rangelands and reinforces our commitment to protecting these fragile ecosystems. The cooperation of the Lachen Dzumsa (traditional local self-governance body) in facilitating access to these remote areas has been important to this work,” Sikkim’s Chief Conservator of Forests (Wildlife), Udai Gurung, said in a press note.

item.title: Centre cuts windfall tax on petrol, diesel and aviation fuel
item.description: The special duty on diesel exports has been cut to Rs 24 from Rs 25.5, on aviation fuel to Rs 19.5 from Rs 22 and on petrol to zero from Rs 3.5.
item.content:encoded:
The Union Finance Ministry has cut the windfall tax on exports of petrol, diesel and aviation turbine fuel from Saturday, according to a gazette notification.

India first imposed the windfall tax in July 2022 to capture extraordinary gains made by oil companies as crude prices surged. The tax was scrapped two years later and reintroduced in March after oil prices rose amid the crisis in West Asia.

The special additional excise duty, through which the windfall tax is levied, has been cut on diesel exports to Rs 24 per litre from Rs 25.5.

The duty on aviation turbine fuel exports has been reduced to Rs 19.5 per litre from Rs 22, while the levy on petrol exports has been cut to zero from Rs 3.5 per litre.

The revised rates took effect on Saturday. There was no change in the existing duty rates on petrol and diesel sold for domestic consumption.

The government imposed the export duty on diesel and aviation turbine fuel on March 27 and has revised the rates every fortnight. The levy was extended to petrol exports from May 16.

The windfall tax is intended to ensure domestic availability of petroleum products and discourage exporters from benefiting excessively from differences between domestic and international prices.
